How to use the app

Five pages; the shared assumptions at the top of three of them apply to all three

Overview. The 7,043 customers, how many left, the price of each service recovered from the bills, and who is at risk.

Pricing (Engine 1). Sets a new price for each of the ten services. Press Run Engine 1; then Run sensitivity to see whether the answer depends on price sensitivity.

Retention (Engine 2). Picks which at-risk customers to call and with which offer, within your budget, agent hours and cap per offer. Export the call list as a CSV for the call centre.

Coupling. Runs Engine 2 at several budgets, then Engine 1 on the lower churn, to show how retention spending frees room to raise prices.

Click any ? next to a label to jump to its entry below. Every result is an expected value under the settings on screen, not a forecast.

Agent time and cost per customer

What one call takes and costs, by offer · costs at the average bill of $64.86 a month

OFFER	AGENT TIME PER CALL	COST IF ACCEPTED	EXPECTED COST PER CALL
One-year contract	0.5 h (30 min)	$77.83	$23.35
Two-year contract	0.75 h (45 min)	$233.49	$70.05
Free tech support	0.5 h (30 min)	$9.05	$2.72
Free online security	0.5 h (30 min)	$9.02	$2.71
Autopay switch	0.5 h (30 min)	$25.00	$7.50
Two-year + tech support	1 h (60 min)	$252.54	$75.76
Agent time is spent on every call, whether or not the customer accepts; the money cost is paid only by those who accept, so the expected cost per call is the cost if accepted × the acceptance rate (30% by default).
Where the costs come from: a contract discount costs the revenue given up (10% off for 12 months, 15% off for 24); a free service costs its unit cost for 6 months; the autopay switch costs a $25 credit; two-year + tech support adds a $10 premium.
The suggested campaign (the defaults on Retention): $30,000, 500 agent hours, at most 350 customers per offer. After a run, the Retention page shows the average expected cost and agent time per customer called.
In the coupling sweep each budget gets agent hours and a cap per offer in the same proportions: one agent hour per $60 and one offer slot per $85.70 of budget.
Terms

In the order you meet them in the app

ChurnOverview

A customer leaving. In this data a customer has churned if they left at some point in their recorded time as a customer. 26.5% of customers did.

TenureOverview

How many months someone has been a customer. The churn model treats it as the time each customer was at risk of leaving.

Recovered price listOverview

The bills are not itemised, so the price of each service is worked out from the bills of customers with different combinations of services (R² 0.9988: the prices explain the bills almost exactly).

Monthly churn risk (hazard)Overview, Retention

The chance that a customer leaves in a given month, given their contract, services, payment method and how long they have been a customer.

At-risk customer (candidate)Overview, Retention

A current customer (not one the data says has already left) whose monthly churn risk is at or above the at-risk threshold (3% a month by default): 740 of the 5,174 current customers at the default. The churn model itself learns from all 7,043 customers, including those who left.

Profit marginShared assumptions

The share of each bill that is profit. Costs are fixed per service at (1 − margin) × today's price, so raising a price raises profit by the full increase.

Discount rateShared assumptions

How much less a dollar of profit next month is worth than one today, per month. It turns a stream of monthly profit into one present value.

Customer lifetime value (CLV)Pricing, Retention

The present value of all the monthly profit a customer is expected to bring before they leave. Higher churn risk means a shorter expected lifetime and a lower CLV.

Lifetime profitPricing, Coupling

The sum of every customer's CLV: the quantity Engine 1 maximises.

Price sensitivity (η)Shared assumptions

How strongly a customer's churn risk rises when their bill rises. It cannot be measured from this data, because no price ever changed, so it is a scenario setting tested from 0.4 to 1.5.

Price boundPricing

How far any single price may move from today's, up or down.

Bill-shock capPricing

How far any customer's total monthly bill may move. It is checked for every combination of services that customers actually hold.

Churn ceilingPricing

The rule that average monthly churn risk may not rise above today's. It is what makes Engine 1 cut fibre: without it, every price simply rises to the bill-shock cap.

Value of 1% churn roomPricing

How much more lifetime profit the best prices would make if the business accepted 1% more average churn. It prices the trade-off; it is not a recommendation.

Sensitivity check (pattern)Pricing

Engine 1 re-solved at four price sensitivities. The pattern has one letter per service: U at the upper price bound, + or − moved up or down inside it.

Retention budgetRetention

The money available for offers, counted as expected cost: what accepted offers will cost on average.

Agent hoursRetention

Total call-centre time available for the campaign. Each call takes the time listed in the table above.

Cap per offerRetention

The most customers who may receive the same offer, so the campaign is not all one offer.

Acceptance rateRetention

The share of called customers who say yes. It is not in the data; 30% comes from published retention studies.

Contract-effect strengthRetention

How much of the churn reduction the model links to longer contracts is believed. Customers who chose long contracts were already less likely to leave, so part of the link is selection, not effect; ×0.5 keeps half of it.

Value preservedRetention

The expected gain in lifetime value from the call list: for each customer, acceptance × (CLV with the offer − CLV today).

LP boundRetention

The best value possible if customers could receive fractions of offers. No real call list can beat it, so it measures how close the actual list is.

Optimality gapRetention

How far the call list's value is below the LP bound. The solver stops at 0.1%; it usually does much better.

Greedy rankingRetention

Sorting customers by a score and calling from the top until the budget, hours or caps run out. The best of three such rankings is compared with the optimiser's list.

Solver time limitRetention, Coupling

The longest the offer optimiser may search. If it stops there, the page says so: the list is the best found in that time, not proven within the gap.

Still called · same offerRetention

From the robustness check: the share of the base list's customers called again under a weaker assumption, and the share of those who get the same offer.

CouplingCoupling

Linking the two engines: retention calls lower some customers' churn, which leaves room under the churn ceiling to raise prices.

Net gainCoupling

Lifetime profit at the new prices and the lower churn, minus the retention spend, minus today's lifetime profit.
Formulas

i = a customer, j = an offer, B = monthly bill, h = monthly churn risk, m = margin, d = discount rate

Customer lifetime value

CLVi = πi / (d + hi), πi = m × Bi

Monthly profit π, discounted, for as long as the customer is expected to stay (profit arrives at the end of each month).

How churn risk responds to a new price list P (Engine 1)

Bi(P) = Σservices held Ps, hi(P) = hi × (Bi(P) / Bi)η

Engine 1: price optimiser

maximise Σi (Bi(P) − Ci) / (d + hi(P)), Ci = (1 − m) × today's Bi

subject to: each price within the price bound; every service combination's bill within the bill-shock cap; fibre at least $10 above DSL; average h(P) ≤ today's average h (churn ceiling, when on).

Engine 2: offer optimiser

Vij = a × (CLVi with offer j − CLVi today), costij = a × cost if accepted
maximise Σ Vij xij with xij ∈ {0, 1}: at most one offer per customer; Σ cost ≤ budget; Σ hoursj ≤ agent hours; customers per offer ≤ cap

a = acceptance rate. An offer lowers the customer's churn risk only for its term (12 or 24 months for contracts, 6 months for free services), then it returns to today's.

Offer costs (if accepted)

contract discount = rate × B × months, free service = 6 × unit cost, autopay = $25 credit

Optimality gap

gap = (LP bound − value) / value

Coupling

hi′ = πi / (CLVi + Vi) − d for each called customer
net gain = lifetime profit(new prices, h′) − retention spend − today's lifetime profit

The lower churn risk h′ is the constant monthly risk that would give the customer the value they have with the offer; Engine 1 is then re-solved with the churn ceiling held at today's level.

Methods

How each number on the screens is computed

Service prices: least-squares regression of each customer's bill on the services they hold; the coefficients are the prices.

Monthly churn risk: a piecewise-exponential survival model, fitted as a Poisson regression on customer-months, with tenure bands 1-6, 7-12, 13-24, 25-48 and 49-72 months.

Engine 1: SciPy SLSQP (sequential quadratic programming) from 8 starting points; the answer is kept only if the starts agree. Its Lagrange multiplier on the churn ceiling gives the value of 1% churn room.

Engine 2: a binary integer program solved by SciPy's milp (HiGHS) to a 0.1% gap; its linear relaxation gives the LP bound; three greedy rankings are solved for comparison.

Sensitivity and robustness: the same engines re-solved with one assumption changed and everything else as on screen; they run as background jobs you can cancel.

Coupling: Engine 2 at each budget, each called customer's churn risk lowered to h′, then Engine 1 re-solved.

Assumptions, limits and verification

What every number rests on, and how it is checked

Assumptions

Churn means "left during the recorded tenure"; the dataset card says "last month", which the file contradicts.
One price sensitivity for every customer; it is a setting, because no price ever changed in the data.
Offer effects are what the churn model associates with each contract or service, not measured effects; no offer was ever made.
Acceptance rate: not in the data; 30% from published studies.
Margin, discount rate, budget, hours and caps are manager inputs, not data.

Never claimed

A measured price sensitivity, or "offer X cuts churn by Y%".
"The campaign will save …": every value is expected, under the settings on screen.
That the price answer comes from the shape of the profit curve: the churn ceiling produces it.
That ranking customers by score matches the optimiser: it is several percent worse.

Verification

Every number above is re-derived from the raw file by automated checks (npm run verify, npm run verify:coupling).
